slides.title: Why do we ask "why"?
slides.text: Asking why helps you learn new things. Ice melts because the sun is warm.

slides.title: It's okay to ask questions
slides.text: It is okay to ask a question when you feel confused. Good thinkers ask lots of questions.

slides.title: Look closely first
slides.text: A bug on the ground might look scary at first. Look closely before you decide — it might just be a tiny ladybug.

slides.title: Same or different?
slides.text: Look closely at two toys to compare them. A ball is round, but a block is square.

slides.title: Real or pretend?
slides.text: A cartoon dragon that breathes fire is pretend. A real dog barking next to you is real.

slides.title: Looking for clues
slides.text: Clues can help you solve a mystery. Wet shoes might mean that it rained outside.

slides.title: Two clues together
slides.text: One clue helps you guess. Two matching clues help even more. Muddy paw prints and a wagging tail both mean your dog was outside.

slides.title: Listening all the way
slides.text: Listen to the whole story before you decide what happened. The middle of a story can change everything.

slides.title: Checking with a grown-up
slides.text: You are not sure if something is true. Ask a grown-up you trust to help.

slides.title: Guess or really know?
slides.text: A guess might turn out to be wrong. Looking closely helps you know for sure.

quiz.question: Why do we ask "why"?
choices: To learn new things
For no reason at all
quiz.explanation: Asking why helps you understand things better.

quiz.question: Is it okay to ask a question when something feels confusing?
choices: Yes, that's smart
No, never ask questions
quiz.explanation: Asking questions helps good thinkers learn.

quiz.question: You see a bug on the ground. What should you do before deciding it's scary?
choices: Look closely at it first
Assume it's scary right away
quiz.explanation: Looking closely helps you know what something really is.

quiz.question: A ball and a block — are they the same shape?
choices: No, one is round and one is square
Yes, they are exactly the same
quiz.explanation: Looking closely helps you spot how things are different.

quiz.question: A cartoon dragon that breathes fire — is that real or pretend?
choices: Pretend
Real
quiz.explanation: Cartoons show pretend things, even exciting ones.

quiz.question: Your shoes are wet. What clue could explain why?
choices: It rained outside
Shoes always get wet for no reason
quiz.explanation: Clues help you figure out what happened.

quiz.question: Muddy paw prints and a wagging tail both hint your dog was outside. Do two matching clues help more than just one?
choices: Yes, two matching clues help more
No, one clue is just as good as two
quiz.explanation: More matching clues make you more sure about what happened.

quiz.question: Your friend starts telling you a story. Should you listen to the whole thing before deciding what happened?
choices: Yes, listen all the way through
No, guess after just the first word
quiz.explanation: Listening to the whole story helps you understand it correctly.

quiz.question: You hear something surprising. What should you do?
choices: Ask a grown-up you trust
Just believe it right away
quiz.explanation: Checking with someone you trust helps you know what is true.

quiz.question: A guess might be wrong. What helps you know for sure?
choices: Looking closely to check
Never checking at all
quiz.explanation: Checking turns a guess into something you really know.

slides.title: Think before you act
slides.text: Stop and think before you act. It helps you make a better choice.

slides.title: Slow down to be sure
slides.text: You count your blocks fast and aren't sure of the number. Counting again slowly helps you know for sure.

slides.title: Sorting things into groups
slides.text: Put your toys into matching groups. All the cars go together, and all the animals go together.

slides.title: Which is more?
slides.text: One plate has 3 cookies. Another plate has 5 cookies. Counting them tells you which plate has more.

slides.title: What comes next?
slides.text: Look at this pattern: red, blue, red, blue. Can you guess what color comes next?

slides.title: Guessing what happens next
slides.text: The sky fills up with big dark clouds. That is a clue that rain might be coming soon.

slides.title: What made it happen?
slides.text: Something always makes things happen. Watering the plant is what made it grow tall.

slides.title: Changing your mind
slides.text: Sometimes you learn something new. It is okay to change your mind about it.

slides.title: Picking the best choice
slides.text: An apple and a candy are both snacks. The apple keeps your tummy full for longer.

slides.title: Try it again if it doesn't work
slides.text: A puzzle piece does not fit in the spot. Try a different piece instead of giving up.

quiz.question: What should you do before you act?
choices: Stop and think first
Just do it right away
quiz.explanation: Thinking first helps you make a better choice.

quiz.question: You count your blocks fast and aren't sure you got it right. What should you do?
choices: Count again slowly to be sure
Just guess and move on
quiz.explanation: Counting again slowly helps you know the real answer.

quiz.question: What is a good way to organize your toys?
choices: Put them into matching groups
Mix them all together
quiz.explanation: Sorting into groups is a first step toward organized thinking.

quiz.question: One plate has 3 cookies, another has 5. Which plate has more?
choices: The plate with 5
They both have the same amount
quiz.explanation: Counting carefully tells you which amount is bigger.

quiz.question: Red, blue, red, blue, red... what comes next?
choices: Blue
Green
quiz.explanation: The pattern repeats red then blue.

quiz.question: The sky fills up with big dark clouds. What might that mean?
choices: It might rain soon
The clouds mean nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Noticing clues like clouds helps you guess what might happen next.

quiz.question: A plant grows tall because you gave it water every day. What made it grow?
choices: Watering it
Nothing made it happen
quiz.explanation: Watering the plant is the cause, and it growing tall is the effect.

quiz.question: You learn something new that shows you were wrong. What should you do?
choices: Change your mind
Never change your mind
quiz.explanation: Learning new things can change what you think, and that is okay.

quiz.question: An apple and a piece of candy are both snack choices. Which one keeps you full longer?
choices: The apple
They are exactly the same
quiz.explanation: Thinking about a choice, not just grabbing the first thing, can lead to a better pick.

quiz.question: A puzzle piece does not fit where you tried it. What should you do?
choices: Try a different piece
Give up right away
quiz.explanation: Trying again, a different way, is how you solve tricky puzzles.

slides.title: Fact vs. opinion
slides.text: A fact is something true that you can check, like 'the sun is hot.' An opinion is what someone feels or believes, like 'summer is the best season.'

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Good thinkers ask follow-up questions instead of just accepting an answer, like 'how do you know that?' If a friend says a game is the best ever, ask what makes it the best.

slides.title: More than one answer
slides.text: Some questions have more than one good answer, so it pays to think of a few options. Picking between reading, playing outside, or building something often leads to a better choice.

slides.title: Spotting an exaggeration
slides.text: Some statements sound like facts but are really big opinions in disguise. "This is the best pizza in the entire universe" can't actually be checked or proven — it just sounds confident.

slides.title: Don't believe everything right away
slides.text: Something isn't automatically true just because it's written down or posted online. A video claiming a trick will make you "super strong instantly" should make you pause and wonder.

slides.title: A picture doesn't tell the whole story
slides.text: A photo only shows one moment, chosen by whoever took it. A picture of a messy room might have been taken right after a fun project, not because someone is messy all the time.

slides.title: Checking with a trusted source
slides.text: When you're not sure if something is true, ask a grown-up or check a trusted book. If a friend says elephants can't jump, a nature book can tell you if that's really true.

slides.title: Checking more than one place
slides.text: If something you read seems surprising, check whether another trusted source says the same thing. When two or three good sources agree, you can trust the information more.

slides.title: Why is someone telling me this?
slides.text: People sometimes share information because it helps them, not just because it's true. An ad for a toy wants you to buy it, so it will only mention the good parts.

slides.title: It's okay to disagree
slides.text: Two people can look at the same thing and see it differently, and that's normal. You might think a book's ending was happy while your friend thinks it was sad, and you can both still be great friends.

quiz.question: "The movie is 90 minutes long" vs "the movie was boring" — which is the fact?
choices: "The movie is 90 minutes long," since it can be checked
"The movie was boring," since it can be checked
quiz.explanation: Facts are checkable and true, unlike opinions, which are personal views.

quiz.question: What is an "opinion"?
choices: What someone thinks or feels
Something that can be proven true or false
quiz.explanation: Opinions are personal views — they can differ from person to person.

quiz.question: A friend says "this game is the best one ever." What's a smart follow-up question?
choices: "What makes it the best?"
Believe it immediately with no questions
quiz.explanation: Asking follow-up questions is a great way to think critically about new information.

quiz.question: You want to spend your free time well — reading, playing outside, or building something. Is there only one right choice?
choices: No, several choices could be good ones
Yes, there's always exactly one right answer
quiz.explanation: Many questions have more than one good answer worth considering.

quiz.question: "This is the best pizza in the entire universe!" — is that a checkable fact or an opinion dressed up big?
choices: An opinion, even though it sounds like a fact
A fact anyone could prove
quiz.explanation: Big, confident-sounding statements can still just be opinions.

quiz.question: Does everything you read online automatically become true?
choices: No, it should be checked
Yes, if it's written down it's always true
quiz.explanation: Being written or posted online doesn't make something automatically true.

quiz.question: A friend says elephants can't jump. How can you find out if that's really true?
choices: Check a trusted book or ask an adult
Just believe your friend, no need to check
quiz.explanation: Trusted sources like books or knowledgeable adults help confirm facts.

quiz.question: You read a surprising claim in one place. What's a smart next step?
choices: Check if another trusted source says the same thing
Believe it because you read it once
quiz.explanation: When multiple good sources agree, the information is more trustworthy.

quiz.question: An ad for a toy only mentions the good parts. Why?
choices: Because the ad wants you to buy the toy
Ads always tell the full, balanced truth
quiz.explanation: It helps to ask why someone is telling you something, and what they might gain from it.

quiz.question: Does disagreeing with a friend mean the friendship is in trouble?
choices: No, respectful disagreement is normal
Yes, friends must always agree on everything
quiz.explanation: People can see things differently and still be good friends.

slides.title: Cause and effect
slides.text: A cause is why something happened, and an effect is what happened because of it. Forgetting to water a plant is the cause, and the plant wilting days later is the effect.

slides.title: Being a detective
slides.text: A good detective checks several clues before deciding what happened, instead of guessing from just one. If a plant is dying, check its sunlight, water, and soil before assuming you know why.

slides.title: Spotting assumptions
slides.text: An assumption is something you believe without checking if it's true. Saying 'he must be fast because he's tall' assumes something about him that might not be true at all.

slides.title: Correlation isn't causation
slides.text: Two things happening at the same time doesn't mean one caused the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both go up in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn.

slides.title: One example isn't proof
slides.text: One example doesn't prove something is always true, even if it seems convincing. Just because one dog you met was friendly doesn't mean every dog you'll ever meet will be friendly too.

slides.title: Big claims need big evidence
slides.text: A huge claim, like "this vitamin cures every sickness," needs strong proof behind it. One person's story isn't enough evidence for a claim that big.

slides.title: Following the thread
slides.text: If a friend says "cats hate water," a good next question is "how do you know?" Asking that a few times in a row often leads back to real evidence, or shows there wasn't much to begin with.

slides.title: Guessing then testing
slides.text: You guess a plant isn't growing well because it needs more light. Moving it to a sunnier spot and watching what happens next actually tests your guess instead of just hoping you're right.

slides.title: Small numbers can trick you
slides.text: Flipping a coin three times and getting heads every time doesn't mean the coin always lands on heads. A few tries can look like a pattern even when it's really just luck.

slides.title: Changing your mind
slides.text: A good thinker isn't afraid to change their mind when new information shows their first idea was wrong. Learning an animal is actually a mammal, not a reptile, is a reason to update your belief.

quiz.question: You forgot to water a plant, and a few days later it wilted. What does "cause and effect" mean here?
choices: Understanding that forgetting to water it (cause) led to it wilting (effect)
A game with no real meaning
quiz.explanation: Cause and effect helps you connect why something happened to what happened next.

quiz.question: A plant is dying. What does a good detective-thinker do before deciding why?
choices: Checks several clues, like sunlight, water, and soil
Guesses after just one clue
quiz.explanation: Good thinking, like good detective work, weighs multiple clues before concluding.

quiz.question: Saying "he must be fast because he's tall" — what is that an example of?
choices: An assumption — believing something without checking
A proven fact
quiz.explanation: Assumptions are beliefs that haven't actually been checked.

quiz.question: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
choices: No, they just happen at the same time
Yes, anything that happens together must be connected
quiz.explanation: Things happening at the same time doesn't mean one causes the other.

quiz.question: One dog you met was friendly. Does that prove every dog you'll ever meet will be friendly too?
choices: No, one example isn't proof
Yes, one example proves it for all dogs
quiz.explanation: A single example isn't strong enough evidence to prove something is always true.

quiz.question: "This vitamin cures every sickness" is a huge claim. What does a claim that big need?
choices: Strong evidence, not just one story
No evidence at all, since it sounds nice
quiz.explanation: Bigger claims need bigger, stronger evidence before you should believe them.

quiz.question: A friend says "cats hate water." What's a good way to check if that's really true?
choices: Keep asking "how do you know?" until you reach real evidence
Repeat it to others without checking
quiz.explanation: Asking how someone knows something can lead you back to real evidence, or reveal there wasn't any.

quiz.question: You guess a plant isn't growing because it needs more light. What should you do next?
choices: Move it to more light and see what happens
Just assume your guess is correct
quiz.explanation: Testing a guess by trying it out is how you find out if it's really true.

quiz.question: You flip a coin 3 times and get heads all 3 times. Does that mean the coin always lands heads?
choices: No, that could just be luck with a few flips
Yes, 3 flips proves it always lands heads
quiz.explanation: A few tries aren't enough to prove a pattern is real instead of coincidence.

quiz.question: Is it okay to change your mind if you learn new information?
choices: Yes, that's what good thinkers do
No, you should never change your mind
quiz.explanation: Updating your thinking based on new evidence is a sign of strong critical thinking.

slides.title: Evaluating evidence
slides.text: Before believing a claim, it helps to ask: what evidence supports it? Is the evidence strong, weak, or missing entirely? For example, if a classmate claims "this energy drink makes you smarter," asking what actual studies or evidence back that up — versus just a company's advertisement — helps you judge whether it's really true.

slides.title: What makes evidence strong?
slides.text: Not all evidence is equally solid — a claim backed by one blog post is much weaker than one backed by ten independent studies that all found the same thing. Before trusting a claim, it's worth asking how much real evidence actually stands behind it, and how independent that evidence is.

slides.title: Checking the source
slides.text: Who is saying this, and why? A source with something to gain from you believing a claim deserves a closer, more careful look. For example, an ad for a supplement claiming it "boosts brainpower" comes from a company that profits if you believe it — which is exactly why it deserves more scrutiny than a neutral science article on the same topic.

slides.title: Correlation isn't causation
slides.text: Just because two things happen around the same time doesn't mean one caused the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer — but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn. For example, if students who play a certain video game also tend to get good grades, that doesn't necessarily mean the game caused the good grades — maybe both are just linked to having more free time at home.

slides.title: Cherry-picking data
slides.text: Cherry-picking means showing only the evidence that supports your point while quietly leaving out the evidence that doesn't. For example, a company's report might highlight the one month sales went up while leaving out the five months they went down, creating a misleading picture from real, but incomplete, numbers.

slides.title: Percent vs. actual numbers
slides.text: A headline like "cases tripled!" sounds alarming, but tripling from 1 case to 3 cases in a school of 2,000 students is barely anything at all. Checking the actual numbers behind a percentage often changes how alarming — or unalarming — a claim really is.

slides.title: Averages can mislead
slides.text: An average can hide a lot — a class 'average score' of 75% might mean everyone scored near 75%, or it might mean half scored 100% and half scored 50%. For example, two classes could both report a 75% average test score, but one class might have every student scoring close to 75%, while the other has half the class acing it and half failing badly — very different situations hidden behind the same number.

slides.title: One story isn't the whole story
slides.text: A single dramatic story can feel more convincing than a pile of boring statistics, even when the statistics tell the truer story. For example, hearing one scary story about a plane crash can make flying feel dangerous, even though the actual data shows that flying is one of the safest ways to travel.

slides.title: Can it be repeated?
slides.text: If an experiment finds a surprising result once, but nobody else can get the same result when they try it again, that's a warning sign the original finding might not be real. Results that hold up when other people repeat the test are far more trustworthy than a one-time surprise.

quiz.question: A classmate claims "this energy drink makes you smarter." What should you check first?
choices: What evidence actually supports it
Nothing — just believe confident-sounding claims
quiz.explanation: Strong claims deserve strong evidence — checking for it is a core critical thinking skill.

quiz.question: A claim backed by one blog post vs. backed by ten independent scientific studies — which is stronger evidence?
choices: Ten independent studies
They're equally strong
quiz.explanation: More independent evidence pointing to the same conclusion is generally stronger than a single, unverified source.

quiz.question: An ad for a "brain-boosting" supplement comes from the company selling it. Why does that matter?
choices: A source with something to gain deserves closer scrutiny
The source of a claim never matters
quiz.explanation: Considering a source's motives is part of evaluating how trustworthy a claim is.

quiz.question: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
choices: No — correlation isn't the same as causation
Yes, if two things happen together one always causes the other
quiz.explanation: Two things happening together doesn't prove one caused the other.

quiz.question: A company's report shows only the one month sales went up, hiding the five months they went down. What's this called?
choices: Cherry-picking data
A completely fair, balanced report
quiz.explanation: Cherry-picking presents real numbers in a misleading way by leaving out inconvenient parts.

quiz.question: A school goes from 1 case of a cold to 3 cases out of 2,000 students, and a headline says "cases tripled!" What's misleading about that?
choices: The percentage sounds scary but the actual numbers are tiny
Nothing — tripling is always a huge, alarming deal
quiz.explanation: A big percentage change can still describe a very small, unalarming real-world number.

quiz.question: Two classes both average 75% on a test, but one has scores clustered near 75% while the other is half 100s and half 50s. What does this show?
choices: Yes, very different sets of numbers can share the same average
No, an average always tells the whole story
quiz.explanation: Averages can look identical while hiding very different underlying patterns.

quiz.question: A dramatic story about a plane crash can make flying feel dangerous, even though data shows flying is very safe. Why?
choices: A vivid story can feel more convincing than statistics, even when it's misleading
Stories are always more accurate than data
quiz.explanation: One memorable story can outweigh solid data in how convincing it feels, even when the data is more reliable.

quiz.question: An experiment gets a surprising result, but no one else can repeat it. What should that make you think?
choices: Be cautious — it might not be a real, reliable effect
Trust it completely since it happened once
quiz.explanation: Results that can't be repeated by others are a warning sign, not solid proof.

quiz.question: Is "lots of people believe it" the same thing as strong evidence?
choices: No, popularity isn't proof
Yes, if enough people believe something it must be true
quiz.explanation: How many people believe a claim says nothing about whether it's actually true.

slides.title: Spotting assumptions
slides.text: An assumption is something believed without proof. Noticing hidden assumptions in an argument helps you judge whether it actually holds up. For example, the argument "he must be good at math because he's Asian" hides an unproven assumption about a whole group of people, which makes the argument weak the moment you notice it.

slides.title: Stereotypes vs. individuals
slides.text: A stereotype is a generalization applied to a whole group, and it says nothing reliable about any one specific person in that group. Assuming a new classmate is bad at sports because of where they're from tells you nothing real about that individual kid.

slides.title: Considering other perspectives
slides.text: Understanding how a situation looks from someone else's point of view often reveals things your own perspective alone would miss. For example, a disagreement between two group project members might look totally different once you understand that one person was juggling other responsibilities the other didn't know about.

slides.title: Everyone has a blind spot
slides.text: Your own experiences quietly shape what problems feel obvious to you and which ones you barely notice. Someone who's never dealt with money trouble might assume budgeting is "just common sense," without realizing how hard it actually is for someone juggling unpredictable bills.

slides.title: Weighing both sides
slides.text: On a genuinely debatable topic, looking fairly at the strongest arguments on both sides — before forming an opinion — leads to more solid conclusions. For example, before deciding your opinion on whether school should start later, actually reading the strongest arguments on both sides — about sleep and about schedules — leads to a more solid opinion than just picking a side because it sounds nice.

slides.title: Groupthink
slides.text: Groupthink happens when a group moves toward agreement so quickly that individual doubts never get voiced out loud. A class might loudly agree a plan is great, even though privately, several students have real concerns they never mention.

slides.title: Thinking for yourself in a group
slides.text: When everyone around you agrees quickly, it can feel easier to go along with the group than to raise a doubt out loud. For example, if a group project is rushing toward a plan you think has a flaw, speaking up — even briefly — gives the group a chance to catch a mistake before it becomes a real problem.

slides.title: Updating your view
slides.text: Being able to say "I was wrong" and change your mind when solid new evidence appears is a strength, not a failure. For example, if you were sure a friend forgot your birthday on purpose, but then learned their phone had been broken all week, updating your opinion based on that new fact is exactly what a careful thinker does.

slides.title: Being wrong doesn't make you dumb
slides.text: A scientist whose theory gets disproven by better evidence isn't a failure — that's exactly how scientific progress works. Treating being wrong as a normal, expected part of learning makes it much easier to update your views instead of defending them out of pride.

quiz.question: What is an "assumption"?
choices: Something believed without proof
A fact that has been proven true
quiz.explanation: Assumptions are unproven beliefs that can weaken an argument if left unchecked.

quiz.question: Assuming a new classmate is bad at sports because of where they're from — is that fair reasoning?
choices: No, a group generalization says nothing about one specific person
Yes, group generalizations always apply to individuals
quiz.explanation: Stereotypes describe imagined groups, not the actual individual in front of you.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to consider other people's perspectives?
choices: It can reveal things your own viewpoint alone would miss
Other perspectives are never worth considering
quiz.explanation: Different viewpoints often surface details a single perspective would overlook.

quiz.question: Someone who's never struggled with money might assume budgeting is 'just common sense.' What does this show?
choices: Your own background can create a blind spot to others' struggles
Everyone experiences every situation in exactly the same way
quiz.explanation: Personal experience shapes what feels obvious to you, and what you might completely miss in someone else's situation.

quiz.question: Before forming an opinion on a genuinely debatable topic like school start times, what should you do?
choices: Look fairly at the strongest arguments on both sides
Only read arguments that already match your opinion
quiz.explanation: Fairly weighing both sides before deciding leads to a more solid, well-reasoned opinion.

quiz.question: A class loudly agrees a plan is great, even though many privately have doubts. What's this called?
choices: Groupthink — going along with the crowd
Careful, independent thinking
quiz.explanation: Groupthink happens when a group reaches agreement quickly without voicing real doubts.

quiz.question: A group is rushing toward a plan you think has a flaw. What does independent thinking suggest doing?
choices: Speaking up, even if it feels uncomfortable
Staying quiet so you don't disrupt the group
quiz.explanation: Raising a doubt, even briefly, gives a group the chance to catch a mistake early.

quiz.question: You were sure a friend forgot your birthday on purpose, but learn their phone was broken all week. What should you do?
choices: Update your belief based on the new information
Keep believing the original idea no matter what
quiz.explanation: Updating a belief when solid new evidence appears is a sign of careful thinking.

quiz.question: A scientist's theory gets disproven by better evidence. Does that make the scientist a failure?
choices: No, updating theories with better evidence is how progress happens
Yes, a disproven theory always means failure
quiz.explanation: Being wrong and updating your view is a normal, healthy part of learning, not a failure.

quiz.question: Saying "she must not like sports because she wears glasses" — what is that?
choices: An unproven assumption
A proven fact
quiz.explanation: This links two unrelated things without any real evidence connecting them.

slides.title: Defining the real problem
slides.text: Sometimes what looks like the problem is actually just a symptom of a different, deeper problem. Defining the real issue is the first step to solving it well. For example, a student who keeps falling asleep in class might seem lazy, but the real problem could be staying up too late — fixing bedtime, not "trying harder to stay awake," is what actually solves it.

slides.title: Root cause vs. quick fix
slides.text: A bike chain that keeps falling off can be oiled again and again, but if the chain itself is stretched out, oiling it is only ever a quick fix. Finding the actual root cause — replacing the stretched chain — solves the problem instead of just delaying it.

slides.title: Breaking a big problem into parts
slides.text: A goal like "get better at math" is so big and vague that it's hard to know where to even start. Breaking it into something specific, like "practice fractions for fifteen minutes a day," turns an overwhelming goal into something you can actually do.

slides.title: Setting a goal and checking progress
slides.text: Deciding what you're aiming for, then regularly checking whether your approach is actually getting you closer, keeps effort from being wasted. For example, if your goal is to improve a test score, checking after a few practice tests whether your study method is actually helping lets you switch strategies early instead of wasting weeks on something that isn't working.

slides.title: Testing your solution
slides.text: After trying a new study method, checking whether your next quiz score actually improved tells you if it really worked — assuming it helped just because it felt different isn't the same as knowing.

slides.title: Working backward from the goal
slides.text: Planning a big project by starting at the deadline and figuring out what needs to happen each week before it often works better than just starting at the beginning and hoping. Working backward from the goal turns a vague deadline into a clear weekly plan.

slides.title: Asking better questions
slides.text: The quality of your thinking often depends on the quality of your questions — a vague question gets a vague answer. For example, instead of asking "is this a good school?" asking "good at what, and good for whom?" forces a much more specific, useful answer than the original question ever could.

slides.title: Ruling out the obvious wrong answer
slides.text: On a hard multiple-choice question, eliminating the choices you already know are wrong first makes the remaining decision much easier. Ruling out bad options is often a faster path to the right one than staring at all of them at once.

slides.title: When to ask for help
slides.text: Being stuck on one problem for thirty minutes without progress is usually a sign that it's a good time to ask for help, not a sign of failure. Knowing when to ask is its own kind of good thinking, not a shortcut around it.

quiz.question: A student keeps falling asleep in class, and the real cause turns out to be a late bedtime. What does "defining the real problem" mean here?
choices: Making sure you're solving the actual issue, not just a symptom of it
Skipping straight to a solution without thinking
quiz.explanation: Solving the wrong problem — even solving it well — doesn't actually help.

quiz.question: A bike chain keeps falling off, and oiling it only helps for a day. What does looking for the root cause mean here?
choices: Figuring out the chain itself is stretched and needs replacing
Oiling it every single day forever without asking why
quiz.explanation: A root cause fix solves the actual issue instead of repeating a temporary patch.

quiz.question: "Get better at math" is a huge, vague goal. What's a smarter way to approach it?
choices: Break it into a specific step, like practicing fractions 15 minutes a day
Just repeat the vague goal to yourself daily
quiz.explanation: Breaking a big goal into a specific, doable step makes it much easier to actually achieve.

quiz.question: Why is checking progress toward a goal useful?
choices: It keeps effort from being wasted on the wrong approach
Checking progress never matters
quiz.explanation: Regularly checking progress lets you adjust before too much effort is wasted.

quiz.question: You change your study method. How do you know if it actually helped?
choices: Check whether your next quiz score actually improved
Just assume it worked because it felt different
quiz.explanation: Checking real results, not just how something felt, tells you if a change actually worked.

quiz.question: Planning a big project by starting at the deadline and figuring out what needs to happen each week before it — what's this approach called?
choices: Working backward from the goal
Waiting until the night before to start
quiz.explanation: Working backward from a deadline turns a vague timeline into a clear, weekly plan.

quiz.question: Which question is more useful: "is this a good school?" or "good at what, and for whom?"
choices: The more specific question — vague questions get vague answers
They are exactly equally useful
quiz.explanation: Specific questions tend to produce much more useful answers than vague ones.

quiz.question: On a hard multiple-choice question, what's a smart first step?
choices: Rule out the choices you know are wrong
Guess immediately without reading the choices
quiz.explanation: Eliminating clearly wrong choices first makes the remaining decision much easier.

quiz.question: You've been stuck on one problem for 30 minutes. What does that usually mean?
choices: It's a good time to ask for help
You should never ask for help, no matter how long you're stuck
quiz.explanation: Recognizing when you're stuck and asking for help is a smart move, not a weakness.

quiz.question: A team keeps missing deadlines and everyone blames laziness, but the real issue is unclear instructions. What should the team fix first?
choices: The unclear instructions, the actual root problem
Nothing, just keep blaming laziness
quiz.explanation: Fixing the real, underlying problem works better than blaming the wrong cause.

slides.title: What is confirmation bias?
slides.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice and believe information that agrees with what you already think, while ignoring information that doesn't. For example, someone convinced a certain diet is unhealthy might notice and remember every negative story about it, while barely registering the many studies showing it's fine — without even realizing they're doing it.

slides.title: Naming the bias helps you catch it
slides.text: Simply knowing a bias's name — like confirmation bias — makes it noticeably easier to catch it happening in your own thinking, in the moment it's happening. Psychologists have named dozens of these predictable mental shortcuts, precisely because naming them is the first step to correcting for them.

slides.title: Availability bias
slides.text: Availability bias is judging how common or dangerous something is by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by the real numbers. After one dramatic news story, shark attacks can feel common, even though they're extremely rare — the vivid story is simply easier to recall than the actual statistics.

slides.title: Negativity bias
slides.text: Negative experiences and information tend to stick in memory far more strongly than positive ones do, a pattern called negativity bias. One harsh comment among ten kind ones is often the single one still bothering you at the end of the day, even though it was a tiny fraction of what was actually said.

slides.title: Self-serving bias
slides.text: Self-serving bias is the tendency to credit yourself for successes while blaming outside factors for failures. Crediting a good grade to "I'm smart" but blaming a bad grade on "the test was unfair" applies two very different standards to two outcomes that might have had the same actual cause.

slides.title: The Dunning-Kruger idea
slides.text: People who know the least about a subject are sometimes the most overconfident about it, simply because they don't yet know enough to see what they're missing. Someone who's watched a few cooking videos can feel more confident than a line cook with years of real kitchen experience, who knows firsthand how much there still is to learn.

slides.title: Anchoring bias
slides.text: Anchoring bias happens when the first number or piece of information you hear quietly shapes every judgment that comes after it, even if that first piece of information was random or irrelevant. For example, a store listing a jacket's "original price" as absurdly high right next to a "sale price" makes the sale price feel like a bargain, even if that original price was never real.

slides.title: The sunk cost fallacy
slides.text: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to keep investing time or money in something just because you've already invested so much, even when quitting would clearly be the smarter choice. For example, finishing a boring movie "because I already sat through an hour of it" ignores the fact that the hour is gone either way, and the only real question is whether the next hour is worth it.

slides.title: Being willing to update
slides.text: Genuinely strong thinkers treat their own conclusions as open to revision — new, credible evidence should be able to change a well-reasoned mind. For example, if you strongly believed a certain study supported your view, but later learned that study was retracted for bad data, updating your opinion in light of that is a sign of strength, not weakness.

quiz.question: Someone convinced a diet is unhealthy notices every negative story but barely registers positive studies. What is this called?
choices: Confirmation bias — favoring information that agrees with what you already believe
Always changing your opinion based on new facts
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias is a natural tendency to seek out agreeing information and dismiss disagreeing information.

quiz.question: Why does it help to know the name of a bias, like 'confirmation bias'?
choices: It makes the bias easier to notice happening in your own thinking
Knowing the name has no effect on noticing it
quiz.explanation: Naming a mental pattern makes it much easier to recognize and correct for.

quiz.question: After one scary news story, shark attacks feel common, even though they're extremely rare. What's this called?
choices: Availability bias — judging by what easily comes to mind, not real numbers
An accurate way to judge how common something is
quiz.explanation: Availability bias mistakes how memorable something is for how common it actually is.

quiz.question: One harsh comment sticks in your memory more than ten kind ones from the same day. What does this show?
choices: Negative experiences tend to stick in memory more strongly
Positive and negative experiences are always remembered equally
quiz.explanation: Negativity bias makes bad experiences disproportionately memorable compared to good ones.

quiz.question: Crediting a good grade to "I'm smart" but blaming a bad grade on "the test was unfair" — what's this?
choices: Self-serving bias
A perfectly balanced, objective view of both grades
quiz.explanation: Self-serving bias applies different standards to your own successes and failures.

quiz.question: Someone who's watched a few cooking videos feels more confident than a chef with years of experience. What does this illustrate?
choices: People who know the least can be the most overconfident
More knowledge always makes people feel less confident
quiz.explanation: Limited knowledge can hide just how much you don't know, inflating confidence.

quiz.question: A store lists a jacket's 'original price' as absurdly high right next to the sale price. What does this exploit?
choices: Anchoring bias — the first number shapes how later numbers feel
Nothing, the original price never affects how we judge the sale price
quiz.explanation: The first number you see quietly shapes how you judge every number after it.

quiz.question: Finishing a boring movie just because you already sat through an hour of it is an example of what?
choices: The sunk cost fallacy
Steelmanning an argument
quiz.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy is letting past investment, which can't be recovered either way, drive a present decision.

quiz.question: Should a strong thinker be willing to change a conclusion?
choices: Yes, if credible new evidence supports it
No, changing your mind is always a weakness
quiz.explanation: Updating conclusions in light of solid new evidence is a hallmark of strong thinking, not weakness.

quiz.question: A person avoids flying because of one dramatic crash story, but keeps using an app just because "I already spent so much time on it." Which two biases are at play, in order?
choices: Availability bias, then the sunk cost fallacy
Confirmation bias, then anchoring bias
quiz.explanation: The crash story looms large due to availability bias, while continuing due to past investment is the sunk cost fallacy.

slides.title: Media literacy
slides.text: Understanding who created a piece of media, why, and who it's meant to persuade helps you judge how much to trust it. For example, an article about a product's benefits written by the company that sells it deserves a different level of trust than an independent review with no financial stake in the outcome.

slides.title: Primary vs. secondary sources
slides.text: A primary source is the original material — a study itself, a direct quote, raw data. A secondary source describes or summarizes that original, like a news article about the study, and can introduce distortion, simplification, or spin along the way, even without meaning to.

slides.title: Follow the money
slides.text: Checking who funded or profits from a piece of information is a fast way to judge how much scrutiny it deserves. A "study" funded by a soda company that finds sugar isn't harmful deserves a closer, more skeptical look than an independent study with no financial stake in the result.

slides.title: Recognizing propaganda
slides.text: Propaganda uses one-sided, emotionally charged messaging to push a viewpoint rather than inform. Learning to notice it helps you separate persuasion from honest information. For example, a message using only scary language and dramatic music to push one specific opinion, while ignoring any counter-evidence entirely, is a sign you might be looking at propaganda rather than balanced information.

slides.title: Loaded language
slides.text: Loaded language uses words chosen to trigger an emotional reaction rather than to describe something neutrally. Calling a policy a "job-killing disaster" instead of "an economic change" can describe the exact same policy while pushing a reader toward a very different feeling about it.

slides.title: Clickbait headlines
slides.text: A headline like "You won't BELIEVE what happened next!" is engineered to provoke a click, not to accurately summarize what follows. Clickbait headlines often overstate, distort, or leave out the actual substance of the story underneath them.

slides.title: Weighing evidence fairly
slides.text: Strong critical thinkers weigh the quality and quantity of evidence on all sides before forming a conclusion — not just picking whichever side feels more comfortable. For example, when researching a controversial topic for a school paper, deliberately reading strong arguments on both sides, not just the ones that confirm what you already believed, produces a far more credible paper.

slides.title: Burden of proof
slides.text: The burden of proof is the idea that whoever makes a claim is responsible for backing it up — not the other way around. For example, if someone claims a supplement cures headaches, it's their job to show real evidence for that, not everyone else's job to prove that it doesn't.

slides.title: Separating feelings from facts
slides.text: Recognizing when a strong emotional reaction — anger, excitement, fear — might be clouding a decision helps you think more clearly under pressure. For example, feeling furious after reading one upsetting headline might push you to share it immediately, but pausing to check the facts first, once the initial anger fades, often changes how you'd respond to it.

slides.title: Checking a claim in three steps
slides.text: A simple habit for evaluating almost any claim: who said it, what's their evidence, and does anyone independent agree. Running a claim through these three questions catches a surprising number of weak or misleading claims before they take hold.

quiz.question: What does "media literacy" involve?
choices: Understanding who made a piece of media and why
Watching as much media as possible without thinking about it
quiz.explanation: Media literacy is about critically evaluating the source and purpose behind media.

quiz.question: A news article summarizes a scientific study. Which one is the primary source?
choices: The original study itself
The news article summarizing it
quiz.explanation: The primary source is the original material; anything describing it is secondary.

quiz.question: A 'study' funded by a soda company finds that sugar isn't harmful. What should that funding make you do?
choices: Look at the study with extra scrutiny
Trust it exactly as much as any independent study
quiz.explanation: Who funds or profits from a claim is relevant to how much scrutiny it deserves.

quiz.question: What is "propaganda"?
choices: One-sided, emotionally charged messaging meant to persuade
A neutral, balanced news report
quiz.explanation: Propaganda pushes a viewpoint through emotional persuasion rather than balanced information.

quiz.question: Calling a policy a "job-killing disaster" instead of "an economic change" — what's this an example of?
choices: Loaded language chosen to trigger emotion
Neutral, objective description
quiz.explanation: Loaded language pushes a reader's feelings rather than describing something plainly.

quiz.question: A headline reads "You won't BELIEVE what happened next!" What is this style of headline designed to do?
choices: Provoke a click, often by overstating the actual story
Accurately summarize the story in a neutral way
quiz.explanation: Clickbait is optimized to generate clicks, not to inform accurately.

quiz.question: When researching a controversial topic for a school paper, what produces a more credible paper?
choices: Deliberately reading strong arguments on both sides
Only reading sources that already agree with you
quiz.explanation: Considering strong arguments from multiple sides leads to a more credible, well-reasoned paper.

quiz.question: Who does the "burden of proof" fall on when someone makes a claim?
choices: The person making the claim
Everyone else, to disprove it
quiz.explanation: Whoever makes a claim is responsible for backing it up with evidence.

quiz.question: Why might a strong emotional reaction be worth noticing during a decision?
choices: It might be clouding clear thinking in the moment
Emotions never affect decision-making at all
quiz.explanation: Recognizing strong emotions helps you separate how you feel from what the facts actually show.

quiz.question: What's a simple three-step habit for checking a claim?
choices: Who said it, what's their evidence, does anyone independent agree
Believe it once, then never think about it again
quiz.explanation: This three-step habit catches a lot of weak or misleading claims quickly.

slides.title: Common logical fallacies
slides.text: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning — like attacking a person instead of their argument, or assuming something is true just because 'everyone believes it.' For example, responding to someone's argument about climate policy by saying "well, you're not even a scientist" attacks the person instead of addressing what they actually said — that's a logical fallacy, not a real rebuttal.

slides.title: The false dilemma
slides.text: A false dilemma presents only two extreme options when more actually exist. "Either you support this exact plan completely, or you don't care about the problem at all" ignores every reasonable middle position between full support and total indifference.

slides.title: The slippery slope
slides.text: A slippery slope argument claims that one small step will inevitably cascade into an extreme outcome, without actually showing why that chain of events would happen. "If we let students retake one quiz, soon nobody will ever study for anything" skips over every reasonable middle possibility in between.

slides.title: Circular reasoning
slides.text: Circular reasoning is an argument that just restates its own conclusion as if that were proof. "This app is the most popular because everyone uses it, and everyone uses it because it's the most popular" goes in a loop without ever landing on any real, independent evidence.

slides.title: Steelmanning an argument
slides.text: Instead of attacking the weakest version of an opposing view, a strong thinker engages with the strongest, most reasonable version of it — called 'steelmanning.' For example, instead of arguing against the silliest version of an opposing political view you've heard, engaging with the most thoughtful argument that side actually makes leads to a much stronger, more honest debate.

slides.title: Building a real argument
slides.text: A solid argument states a clear claim, backs it with real evidence, and directly addresses the strongest objection to it — not just the loudest or weakest voice in the room. Arguments that skip the third step tend to fall apart the moment someone raises a serious counterpoint.

slides.title: Deciding under uncertainty
slides.text: Many real decisions have to be made without knowing everything for certain. Thinking in terms of likely outcomes, not guaranteed ones, leads to better choices. For example, choosing a college major isn't about finding a guaranteed-perfect choice — it's about weighing which path seems most likely to lead somewhere you'd be happy, given what you know now.

slides.title: Expected value, informally
slides.text: A good decision weighs not just whether an outcome would be good or bad, but how likely it actually is. A tiny chance at a huge reward can, depending on the actual numbers, be worth less than a near-certain chance at a merely decent one — it's the combination of size and likelihood that matters, not either alone.

slides.title: The scientific method, briefly
slides.text: Form a question, propose an explanation, test it, and revise based on results — this basic loop underlies careful thinking far beyond just science class. For example, if you wonder "does studying with music help or hurt my focus," you could test it by studying with music some days and without on others, then honestly comparing your results — the same basic loop scientists use.

slides.title: Sample size and small numbers
slides.text: A pattern based on just a few examples — a 'small sample' — can be pure coincidence rather than a real trend, so bigger samples are generally more trustworthy. For example, if three people from a certain town happen to be tall, that says almost nothing about the town in general, but if a study measures three thousand people from that town, the result actually starts to mean something.

quiz.question: What is a "logical fallacy"?
choices: A flaw in the structure or reasoning of an argument
Any statement that happens to be false
quiz.explanation: Logical fallacies are reasoning errors that can make even a false conclusion sound convincing.

quiz.question: "Either you support this exact plan completely, or you don't care about the problem at all" — what's wrong with this?
choices: It's a false dilemma — it ignores every middle option
Nothing, every issue really only has two possible sides
quiz.explanation: A false dilemma hides the reasonable middle ground between two extremes.

quiz.question: "If we let students retake one quiz, soon nobody will ever study for anything" — what fallacy is this?
choices: A slippery slope — assuming one step must cascade to an extreme, without showing why
A well-supported, logical prediction
quiz.explanation: Slippery slope arguments assume an extreme chain reaction without actually demonstrating it.

quiz.question: "This app is the most popular because everyone uses it, and everyone uses it because it's the most popular." What's wrong with this argument?
choices: It's circular — it never actually offers real evidence
It's a strong argument with solid evidence
quiz.explanation: Circular reasoning restates the conclusion as its own proof instead of offering real evidence.

quiz.question: What does "steelmanning" an argument mean?
choices: Engaging with the strongest version of an opposing view
Ignoring opposing views entirely
quiz.explanation: Steelmanning means fairly addressing the best version of the other side's argument.

quiz.question: What does a solid argument need, beyond just a claim?
choices: Real evidence and a response to the strongest objection
Just being stated loudly and confidently
quiz.explanation: A solid argument needs evidence and must hold up against the best counterargument.

quiz.question: Why is deciding "under uncertainty" a real skill, like choosing a college major?
choices: Most real decisions don't come with guaranteed outcomes
Every decision in life comes with a guaranteed correct answer
quiz.explanation: Thinking in terms of likely outcomes, not certainties, reflects how real decisions actually work.

quiz.question: A tiny chance at a huge reward versus a near-certain chance at a decent reward — what should a good decision weigh?
choices: Both how good the outcome is and how likely it is
Only how good the outcome could be, ignoring likelihood
quiz.explanation: Good decisions under uncertainty weigh both the size of an outcome and its probability.

quiz.question: What is the basic loop of the scientific method?
choices: Question, propose an explanation, test it, revise based on results
Guess once and never check again
quiz.explanation: This loop of testing and revising ideas underlies careful thinking generally, not just science.

quiz.question: Three people from a small town happen to be tall. Does that prove the town is full of tall people?
choices: No — a small sample can just be coincidence
Yes, any pattern you notice is automatically true
quiz.explanation: Small samples can look like a real pattern purely by chance; larger samples are more trustworthy.
